The digital advertising landscape is shifting as artificial intelligence transforms how users find information and connect online. Choosing between Alphabet (GOOGL +1.55%) (GOOG +1.62%) and Meta Platforms (META +0.30%) requires weighing search dominance against social media scale.
Alphabet remains the primary gateway to the internet through its Google search engine and YouTube, while Meta dominates the social landscape with its massive family of apps. Both companies rely heavily on advertising revenue, but their paths to growth in artificial intelligence and the future of hardware are beginning to diverge significantly for investors of the communication sector.
Alphabet operates as a diversified technology holding company, primarily selling digital advertising space through its dominant Search platform and YouTube. It also provides cloud computing services to businesses and develops the Android operating system to support its mobile ecosystem.
In its 2025 fiscal year (FY), revenue reached $402.8 billion, representing a year-over-year growth of 15.1%. This expansion helped drive a net income of $132.2 billion, which was significantly higher than the profit recorded in the previous year. The net margin, which measures how much of each dollar in sales is kept as profit after all expenses, improved to 32.8% compared to the prior period.
As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is 0.1x, indicating that total debt is very low relative to shareholder equity. The current ratio stands at 2.0x, which means the company has twice as many short-term assets as short-term liabilities to cover its bills. Free cash flow for FY 2025 was $73.3 billion, which is the cash generated after paying for operations and capital expenditures.
Meta Platforms builds technologies for human connection through its family of apps, including Facebook, Instagram, and WhatsApp. The company primarily generates revenue by selling highly targeted advertising space to marketers and creators who want to reach its billions of global users. It also offers consumer hardware products through its Reality Labs division, where it maintains complex relationships with mobile operating system providers such as Apple (AAPL +1.02%) and Google that influence its advertising effectiveness.
In FY 2025, revenue reached $201.0 billion, which indicates a robust growth rate of 22.2% from the prior year. Despite this revenue growth, net income was $60.5 billion, which was slightly lower than the profit recorded in the previous year. The net margin for the company was 30.1%, showing it remains highly profitable even as it spends on new initiatives, such as AI data centers.
As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is 0.4x, suggesting a conservative amount of debt compared to its equity. The current ratio is 2.6x, providing a healthy cushion for the company to meet its immediate financial obligations with its existing assets. Free cash flow for the year was $46.1 billion.
Alphabet faces significant regulatory challenges, including a final judgment in a Department of Justice case that may require sharing search data or structural changes. The business is also sensitive to economic downturns that could reduce advertising spending across its Google search and YouTube platforms. Furthermore, the company must manage high capital costs for artificial intelligence infrastructure while facing competition from rivals such as Microsoft.
Meta recently settled a multistate lawsuit for $17.1 billion, which requires the company to implement sweeping child-safety reforms on its social platforms. It also faces ongoing risks from changes in mobile operating systems made by partners like Apple, which can limit the effectiveness of its advertising tools. Additionally, the Reality Labs segment continues to report persistent operating losses as the company tries to develop its long-term hardware and metaverse strategy.
While Meta Platforms offers higher top-line growth, Alphabet trades at a higher valuation multiple based on future earnings estimates and sales. Alphabet and Meta depend on digital advertising to support their businesses, yet both are looking to artificial intelligence to fuel success in future years. Alphabet is spending so much on building out its AI infrastructure, it reported negative free cash flow of $5.9 billion in the second quarter of 2026, as capital expenditures nearly doubled year over year to $44.9 billion.
Meta has fared better despite also nearly doubling capex, as its Q2 free cash flow totaled $784 million. However, that was a steep decline from 2025's free cash flow of $8.5 billion.
Yet that spending may be worth it. Meta's recent release of its Muse AI assistant achieved five million downloads in 22 days, more than popular AI tools such as ChatGPT. Even so, I would invest in Alphabet rather than Meta.
That's because Alphabet has so many ways in which it can employ AI to deliver business growth. Its Waymo autonomous ride-hailing business relies on AI as the driver for its vehicles. The company's cloud computing division, Google Cloud, through which it delivers its proprietary AI models to customers for a fee, experienced 82% year-over-year sales growth to $24.8 billion. This rapid rise in revenue indicates clients are adopting Alphabet's AI offerings, suggesting its capex spending can pay off in the long run.

The simple reason Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg is winning for investors again
For the better part of a year, Meta (META) founder Mark Zuckerberg has been in what techies call founder mode.
And for Zuck, there is much more to being in founder mode than showing up at product demos in comfy clothing as if he's pulling office all-nighters like fellow billionaire Elon Musk.
Founder mode, at its core, is being freakishly locked into executing on a long-term vision literally every second of the day. It's a true obsession with the work at hand.
Provided you're a founder with money — such as Zuck — one component of this mode is being ruthless about hiring the people you need for battle. Money is no object. Where that person currently works is irrelevant. If they fit the job description and can put wins on the board, that's all that matters.
Out comes the checkbook and powers of persuasion.
Zuck was at it again this week, snagging MongoDB (MDB) CEO CJ Desai to help bring Meta's AI tools to businesses. The fact that this happened a day before a MongoDB investor day underscores how ruthless Zuck is being back in the driver's seat. MongoDB — no small-cap company by any means — saw its stock crash.
No matter to Zuck. He got his guy.
"This is Mark. Mark has got the memo, man. He will personally go out and eat with you. He'll deliver soup to you. He'll do whatever it takes to get the right people because he knows the talent is what drives the business like his," former longtime Meta CTO Mike Schroepfer told me on Yahoo Finance's Sozzi Unleashed. Schroepfer is still an adviser to Zuckerberg while also founding tech investment firm Gigascale Capital.
Before the Desai poaching, Zuckerberg spent an eye-popping $14.3 billion to buy up all the employees of hot AI startup Scale AI in 2025. That included well-connected wunderkind Alexandr Wang, who got about $5 billion as part of the deal.
He also hired away scores of other top Silicon Valley minds with lucrative pay packages.
The fruits of Zuck's intensity are now paying off for Meta and its investors.
Meta's new Muse AI agent — which Wang is up all hours of the night posting about on X — has been downloaded more than 5.1 million times so far in its short time in the market.
Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg presents the Muse Charm during the Meta Connect event at the company's headquarters in Menlo Park, Calif., on Sept. 23, 2026. (Reuters/Carlos Barria) · Reuters / REUTERS
Meta also debuted the Muse Charm last week. This is a standalone pocket device built exclusively for voice interaction with the company's Muse agent.
Zuckerberg also showcased a major shift toward "personal superintelligence" by unveiling a hardware-meets-AI moment in the Meta VR Glasses.
Weighing just 100 grams — roughly one-fifth the weight of Meta's Quest 3 — the $1,299 spatial computing glasses feature 5K micro-OLED displays, tethered puck processing, and native eye and hand tracking.
On the smart eyewear front, Meta debuted the third-generation Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3 glasses, starting at an entry-level $249. Joining them are the camera-free Ray-Ban Meta Audio glasses, designed purely for open-ear listening and AI voice interaction.
Meta's stock is up 25% inside of a month. Prior to this run, the stock was down double digits on the year as investors fretted about rising AI capex.
Now that spending may be taken in stride by investors, given that they can tangibly see what Meta is building and its monetization potential.
Score one for founder mode.

Meta Platforms (META) Stock Jumps 27% After Muse Download Surge and Legal Settlement
Meta (META) stock jumped 27% in a month as its Muse AI agent surges past 5 million downloads and legal settlements ease pressure.
By Trader EdgeOctober 2, 20264 Mins Read
Meta’s stock has climbed 27% over the past four weeks, though it’s still down about 1% over the past 12 months.
The company’s new AI agent, Muse, has topped iOS download charts and reportedly passed 5 million downloads.
Meta launched a new Meta Enterprise Platform to sell AI tools to other businesses.
Meta settled many state lawsuits over alleged harm to young users, agreeing to pay up to $18 billion over a decade.
QRG Capital Management increased its Meta stake by 5.5% in the second quarter, and Wall Street holds a “Moderate Buy” rating with a $787.86 average price target.
Meta Platforms (META) stock closed at $725.93 on Friday, up 0.1% on the day. The stock has gained 27% over the past month, a sharp turnaround after a rough stretch.
Over the past 12 months, META is still down roughly 1%. But recent momentum suggests the tide may be turning.
Much of the renewed interest centers on Muse, Meta’s personalized AI agent released on September 8. It quickly became one of the most downloaded apps in the U.S.
Reports now say Muse has surpassed 5 million downloads. JPMorgan analysts noted the free-access approach could pressure subscription rivals while opening new advertising and commerce opportunities.
Muse is free up to a point, with a paid tier for extra features. But the bigger opportunity may be commerce.
Meta has said it plans to charge merchants when Muse helps users complete purchases. That could turn a popular app into a real revenue engine, assuming adoption keeps growing.
The company is also expanding Muse for small businesses, tying AI tools directly to advertising and sales. That’s a logical next step for a company that still earns most of its money from ads.
Competition is heating up fast, though. OpenAI launched its own personal AI agent, Dots, and Google and Apple are reportedly working on similar products too.
Meta also announced a new venture on September 28 called Meta Enterprise Platform. It will sell AI tools and software to other companies, built on the same infrastructure Meta has used internally.
The company already has deep relationships with businesses through its advertising ecosystem. That could give it a head start over newer entrants.
Meta has also cleared up a chunk of its legal overhang. The company settled many lawsuits brought by a bipartisan group of state attorneys general over alleged harm to young users.
Meta agreed to pay up to approximately $18 billion over a decade, with part of that contingent on actions by YouTube and TikTok. It will also add new protections for teens on its apps.
More lawsuits remain, but resolving this major group of claims removes a source of uncertainty that weighed on the stock.
On the institutional side, QRG Capital Management increased its Meta position by 5.5% in the second quarter. The fund now holds 372,579 shares worth about $209.9 million.
Other funds made smaller moves too. Advantage Trust Co, Philadelphia Investment Partners, and Axiom Investment Management all opened new positions during the quarter.
Analysts remain largely positive. Meta carries a “Moderate Buy” consensus rating with an average price target of $787.86, even as some firms have trimmed their targets.
Not everything is rosy. Meta’s AI spending is expected to top $130 billion, and free cash flow has declined as a result.
Insider selling has also drawn attention. COO Javier Olivan and board member Christopher Cox both sold shares in late September under pre-arranged trading plans.
Meta last reported earnings on July 29, posting $6.18 EPS against estimates of $7.19. Revenue came in at $60.80 billion, above the $60.22 billion analysts expected, with quarterly revenue up 28% year over year.

Unity Software jumped after announcing day-one support for Meta's next-generation VR headset, but a timely product catalyst and a struggling business are not the same thing, and traders now face the harder question of which one matters more.
Published September 30, 2026, 2:12pm ET · 3 min read

Unity Software (NYSE:U | U Price Prediction) stock rose 5% to $41.56 as traders weighed the company’s newly announced day-one support for Meta VR Glasses. The product news arrives as Unity works to reinforce its role in extended-reality development, though concerns around sales growth and billings still give investors reasons to remain selective.
The broader software group also moved higher. The iShares Expanded Tech-Software Sector ETF (BATS:IGV) gained 1.5% to $106.81, while the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSE ARCA:SPY) added 0.41% to $767.30.
Unity announced immediate engine support for Meta VR Glasses, Meta Platforms’ next-generation virtual-reality device that is expected to reach retail customers in spring 2027. Unity said developers can begin building and testing experiences now, providing more time to prepare titles for the device’s launch.
For existing Quest developers, Unity said projects built with OpenXR can carry forward with minimal changes. The company also highlighted support for eye and hand tracking, quad views rendering that can reduce GPU demands, and spatial-audio tools designed for more immersive experiences.
Unity’s early compatibility could make the engine more attractive to studios planning games, entertainment products, training software, and other immersive applications for Meta VR Glasses. The company said developers can test certain VR Glasses interactions within the Unity Editor before receiving physical hardware.
Meta Platforms (NASDAQ:META) is central to the opportunity because Meta VR Glasses will sit within the same ecosystem as Meta’s existing Quest products. Unity said existing Quest apps can run on VR Glasses from day one, which could reduce development friction for studios already using Unity’s tools.
That compatibility matters because developers typically prefer to reuse assets, workflows, and code across multiple devices when possible. Unity’s product announcement emphasized a single codebase that can support multiple platforms, potentially helping studios reach additional players without rebuilding projects from scratch.
The opportunity, however, depends on adoption after Meta brings VR Glasses to market. Unity may need to demonstrate that developers are using the new tools, launching successful projects, and expanding their subscriptions or platform spending before the announcement becomes a meaningful financial catalyst.
Adobe (NASDAQ:ADBE) stock climbed 3% to $239.37, adding to the software-sector strength. Adobe remains closely associated with creative and document software, making Adobe stock a familiar way for investors to track demand for productivity tools and AI-enhanced workflows.
Intuit (NASDAQ:INTU) stock gained 2% to $273.21 as software names broadly advanced. Intuit operates consumer and business-focused financial software platforms, and Intuit stock can respond to expectations for customer growth, recurring revenue, and operating leverage.
The gains in Adobe stock and Intuit stock helped show that Unity’s move was not occurring in complete isolation. Still, Unity’s 5% rise outpaced both peers and the IGV ETF, suggesting that the Meta VR Glasses news gave traders a company-specific reason to focus on Unity.
Unity Stock: Growth Questions Remain Important
The positive product headline does not eliminate the concerns surrounding Unity’s underlying business performance. Recent commentary has pointed to stagnant sales, slower billings growth, and a stock that has remained under pressure despite the latest 5% advance.
Unity’s long-term case may depend on whether new platform support translates into broader Create-segment demand and more durable revenue growth. The company has a clear technical story around VR Glasses, yet investors will likely want evidence that product momentum is producing measurable business results.
For now, Unity stock has a timely catalyst, while Adobe stock and Intuit stock are participating in a broader software-sector rally. Investors should watch for signs that Unity’s VR Glasses support leads to new developer adoption, launch titles, and stronger financial metrics, while keeping position sizes modest given the company’s execution risks.

pages.title: Nebius Group signs $27B AI capacity deal with Meta Platforms
pages.text:
Nebius Group signs $27B AI capacity deal with Meta Platforms
The five-year agreement dwarfs a prior $3 billion contract between the two companies and positions Nebius as a major force in AI infrastructure beyond the hyperscaler giants.
Nebius Group just locked in one of the largest AI infrastructure contracts on record. The Netherlands-based company signed a five-year deal with Meta Platforms worth up to approximately $27 billion, a figure that would make it one of the most significant commitments a non-hyperscaler has ever secured from a Big Tech partner.
The deal includes $12 billion in dedicated GPU capacity and up to $15 billion in additional AI capacity purchases, contingent on that capacity remaining unsold to other customers.
The $12 billion dedicated portion of the contract will deploy Nvidia’s Vera Rubin platform, the next-generation GPU architecture that’s becoming the backbone of frontier AI training workloads. Deployments are expected to begin in early 2027 across Nebius data center locations in Finland, the UK, and the US.
The remaining $15 billion functions as a backstop mechanism. If Nebius can’t sell certain capacity to third-party customers, Meta steps in to absorb it. For Nebius, this essentially creates a revenue floor. For Meta, it guarantees access to compute resources without the capital expenditure headache of building every rack itself.
To put the scale in perspective, Nebius signed a $3 billion contract with Meta just four months prior, in November 2025. Going from $3 billion to $27 billion is a ninefold increase in commitment.

pages.title: Meta's Muse AI: Good or Bad for E-Commerce? Shopify and Amazon Are Taking Opposite Approaches. | The Motley Fool
pages.text:
▲ S&P 500 +---%|▲ Stock Advisor +---%Join The Motley Fool
Meta Platforms (META +0.30%) is pushing on the gas pedal for its new artificial intelligence (AI) agent, Muse. Since launching on Sept. 8, the mobile app has accumulated more than 5 million downloads, according to Sensor Tower estimates. With Meta putting its marketing power behind the app, that number could climb even faster over the next few weeks.
Muse is designed to help users get things done. In his keynote address at Meta Connect last week, CEO Mark Zuckerberg said Muse will make people money. That could come in the form of canceling unused subscriptions, finding unclaimed property, or, more likely, being a smarter online shopper.
But not everyone is on board with agentic shopping. Amazon (AMZN +1.32%), the world's largest online retailer, blocked Muse from its platform. Meanwhile, Shopify (SHOP +1.54%), which helps brands build their own e-commerce sites, has fully embraced agentic commerce and is among the many partners Muse has attracted since its launch.
Here's why the e-commerce leaders are diverging, and what it means for investors in Meta, Amazon, and Shopify.
Image source: Getty Images.
Will Muse improve sales for its e-commerce partners?
If Muse makes shopping online faster and easier, it seems likely that customers will spend more online. On the face of it, that seems to benefit any retailer plugging into Muse and other AI agents.
Shopify stands to benefit by making integration extremely easy for small retailers, increasing the value of using its platform. But it stands to benefit even more if more of the gross merchandise value sold online goes through ShopPay, its payment platform. The checkout option is ubiquitous across Shopify-built e-commerce sites, removing the friction of typing in payment information for every small merchant an online shopper might encounter these days.
Shopify's merchant solutions are the largest and fastest-growing segment of its business, and that growth is largely fueled by its payment platform. That makes finding any way possible to get its merchants' products in front of potential customers its No. 1 objective right now. As customers shop from more merchant websites, ShopPay becomes increasingly valuable, and its penetration of gross merchandise value increases. As such, Shopify may be willing to share some revenue with Meta, producing a win-win situation for both companies.

Amazon could also benefit from increased sales on its website. However, the cost of sales through an AI agent like Muse could far outweigh the benefits. That's because Amazon has built a massive advertising business that's generated $76 billion over the last 12 months. That may only be 12% of its total retail operations revenue, but that's high-margin revenue. It's what's helped drive Amazon's overall operating margin significantly higher over the last few years.
If more people use artificial intelligence agents to crawl Amazon's platform, that's potentially fewer opportunities to influence shoppers with advertisements. That means agentic AI is a huge threat to Amazon and any other retailer that derives a significant portion of its profits from retail media advertising. That includes Walmart, which has used advertising as a key source of profit growth over the last few years.
Meta won't be the only company releasing an AI agent like Muse. As agentic AI becomes increasingly accessible, Amazon could lose market share to smaller competitors.
$1.9TMarket cap calculated using publicly traded shares outstanding only. Does not include unlisted, private, or dual-class non-traded shares. Implied market cap may vary.
Can Amazon overcome Meta?
Investors trying to determine how big a threat Muse and other agentic shopping services could be to Amazon need to consider Amazon's competitive advantages. It holds several advantages that could make it more valuable to AI agents than AI agents are to Amazon.
First, it has a massive logistics network that's capable of delivering millions of different items to U.S. households within hours. Customers used to that convenience are unlikely to give it up easily, even if Muse removes the task of searching for and ordering an item.
Second, Amazon holds a tremendous amount of shopping and purchase data on its hundreds of millions of customers. Likewise, it has high-quality data on the products listed on its website, including customer reviews and exact details for each item variation. While Meta also knows a lot about its users, as do other AI developers, Amazon has far more valuable information about its shoppers' preferences. That could make using Amazon's first-party shopping agent much more appealing for most shoppers.
Finally, Amazon has tens of millions of Prime members. Prime is an extremely effective loyalty program, as it offers access to fast, free shipping and other benefits, such as streaming media. That makes Amazon the first place shoppers go, and they may check Muse or another agent that aggregates e-commerce listings as a secondary option.

There are multiple ways Amazon exercises its power. It could drive more merchants to use its logistics network, further increasing its value and pricing power, and pushing its merchant services revenue higher. It could strike deals with AI agents to allow access to its platform, but include sponsored listings in the results. Finally, Amazon may simply push more users to its own agentic platform, where it controls the user experience.
If Muse increases the total amount of online commerce, that can be good for both Shopify and other Meta partners, as well as Meta itself, but it might not pose as big a threat to Amazon, given that its biggest competitive advantage is its physical fulfillment network. That's not something easily replicated. Meanwhile, brick-and-mortar retailers could end up some of the biggest losers, so it's no wonder we're seeing some of the largest retailers partner with Meta to ensure they remain relevant.

pages.title: Meta is building one of the world’s biggest undersea cable networks—it’s just one piece of a growing seafloor empire spanning 6 continents
pages.text:
Skip to navigation Skip to main content Skip to right column
Meta is building one of the world’s biggest undersea cable networks—it’s just one piece of a growing seafloor empire spanning 6 continents
While data centers dominate headlines amid mounting local opposition over electricity bills, water use, and zoning fights, Meta has been expanding its infrastructure somewhere far less visible: the bottom of the ocean.
On Sept. 21, the company announced Petal, a roughly 4,300-mile subsea cable connecting the U.S. and France. Meta says the cable, expected to enter service in 2029, will be the first to deliver petabit-scale capacity across an ocean. It will carry 1 petabit per second, or about 125,000 gigabytes per second, double what today's most advanced transoceanic cables can handle.
According to Meta, that's enough capacity for three-quarters of the world's population to stream music at the same time. The company says Petal achieves this with two-core fiber, which fits two light paths inside each strand. That lets Meta double capacity without a proportional increase in power or physical infrastructure.
Projects like this rarely make headlines in an industry fixated on AI models and apps, but they're what make those products run. Meta's personal AI agent, Muse, launched Sept. 8 and climbed to No. 1 on Apple's U.S. App Store within two weeks, overtaking ChatGPT. It did so even as critics questioned how much access the agent needs to users' email, calendars, and payment accounts. Muse is powered by Meta's Muse Spark models, and products like it depend on moving enormous volumes of data between Meta's data centers and its users around the world.
Subsea cables aren't new territory for the company, which is now valued at roughly $1.85 trillion. Meta has spent the past decade building its presence on the seafloor and says it has invested in more than 20 subsea cable projects. Taken together, those projects touch every continent except Antarctica.
The most ambitious is Project Waterworth, announced in February 2025. Meta says the system will stretch more than 31,000 miles, longer than the Earth's circumference. It will connect the U.S., Brazil, South Africa, India, and other regions across five continents. Some segments will be laid as deep as roughly 4.3 miles below the surface to protect them from ship anchors and other hazards.
Meta's 2Africa system, whose core was completed last year, circles the African continent and connects to Europe, the Middle East, and South Asia. Meta says it lands in 33 countries and can reach 3 billion people.
Meta hasn't built all of this alone. Petal is being developed with Japan's NEC and Sumitomo Electric Industries, and French telecom Orange is handling the landing on France's Atlantic coast. Meta has even partnered with rivals. The MAREA cable between Virginia and Spain, completed in 2017, is jointly owned with Microsoft and telecom company Telxius. Increasingly, though, Meta is taking the driver's seat. Waterworth will be wholly owned by Meta, making it only the company's third solely owned cable, according to telecom research firm TeleGeography.
These projects don't come cheap. Meta hasn't disclosed what Petal or Waterworth will cost, but TechCrunch reported before Waterworth's announcement that the project could top $10 billion. Even so, cables are a small slice of Meta's overall infrastructure bill. The company expects capital expenditures of $130 billion to $145 billion this year, nearly double the $72.2 billion it spent in 2025.
With 12-figure budgets and record-breaking construction projects, Meta is betting its infrastructure spending will pay off. Whether it does remains to be seen.

Meta Platforms stock (ISIN US30303M1027) last closed at USD 648.03 on Nasdaq on September 11, 2026, leaving the company valued at about USD 1.65 trillion and giving investors a visible AI-driven rerating story around its new Muse agent and ongoing legal settlement effects.
Muse AI and settlement sharpen the growth story
According to Investing.com on September 14, 2026, Goldman Sachs reiterated its Buy rating on Meta Platforms and kept a 12-month price target of USD 725, stating that it views the stock with increased conviction after Meta agreed to settle litigation over its services for minors and launched its new Muse AI agent.
As Sina Finance reported on September 14, 2026, Goldman Sachs highlighted Muse AI as a shift from simple chatbots toward intelligent agents that can autonomously execute real-world tasks, and it calculated that the USD 725 target implies 11.9% upside from the reference price of USD 648.03.
For investors, the key takeaway is that the combination of a resolved legal overhang and a new class of AI products has turned Muse into a central medium-term catalyst, even as some analysts still express caution about the timing of monetization.
Q2 2026 earnings show strong revenue, weaker margins
Meta Platforms has already reported results for the second quarter of its fiscal year ending December 2026, covering the period from April to June 2026.
According to an earnings analysis from Rakuten Securities on September 14, 2026, Meta generated revenue of USD 60.801 billion in Q2 2026, an increase of 28.0% compared with the same quarter of the prior year.
The same report from Rakuten Securities noted that operating income in Q2 2026 reached USD 18.775 billion, which represented an 8.2% decline year on year as sharply higher research and development spending and roughly USD 2.4 billion in litigation-related costs weighed on profitability.
Looking at the core advertising business, Rakuten Securities reported that advertising revenue rose 27.5% year on year to USD 59.363 billion in Q2 2026, while the Family of Apps segment delivered USD 60.370 billion in revenue and USD 23.394 billion in operating profit, the latter falling 6.3% from the prior-year quarter.
The same analysis also pointed out that Meta guided for Q3 2026 revenue in a range of USD 61 billion to USD 64 billion, which corresponds to year-on-year growth between 19.0% and 24.9%, but it cautioned that new restrictions on social media use by minors in the United States could start to weigh on advertising growth from Q3 onward.
Consensus points to double-digit upside despite skepticism on Muse
Wall Street remains broadly positive on Meta Platforms despite debate about how quickly Muse and other AI agents will translate into revenue.
According to MarketBeat as of September 13, 2026, Meta Platforms carries a consensus rating of Moderate Buy based on 4 Strong Buy ratings, 34 Buy ratings and 9 Hold ratings, and it has an average analyst price target of USD 787.54, implying around 21.5% upside from the closing price of USD 648.03.
The same overview from MarketBeat shows a 52-week trading range between USD 520.26 and USD 790.80 for Meta stock, which situates the recent price roughly in the middle of that band and still about 18.1% below the 52-week high.
As StockAnalysis reported on September 13, 2026, a separate compilation of Wall Street estimates points to an average price target of USD 754.15, about 16.4% above the same USD 648.03 reference price, and classifies the stock with a Strong Buy consensus based on 62 analyst opinions.
For investors, the quantified gap between the current share price and the analyst target range in the mid-700s to low-800s underscores that the Street is still assigning significant value to Meta's AI roadmap, even if individual houses differ in how aggressively they factor Muse and other agentic products into their models.
Analyst actions around Muse highlight both optimism and risk
Recent individual analyst calls around Muse illustrate the spectrum from enthusiasm to caution.
As Blockonomi reported on September 14, 2026, Wedbush analyst Ygal Arounian maintained a Hold rating on Meta but raised his price target by 9% from USD 595 to USD 650 on September 11, 2026, leaving only about 0.3% upside versus the prevailing trading level and signaling a more cautious stance on Muse's near-term revenue contribution.
The same article from Blockonomi noted that Evercore ISI reiterated an Outperform rating with a price objective of USD 860, JPMorgan upgraded Meta from Neutral to Overweight with a new target of USD 820, and KeyBanc kept an Overweight rating alongside a USD 780 target, all citing AI advances including Muse and the Meta Model application programming interface as key drivers.
Across the broader sell-side landscape, Blockonomi summarized that Meta currently enjoys a Strong Buy consensus built on 38 Buy ratings and 6 Hold ratings over the past three months, with an average price target of USD 759.43 that implies about 17% potential upside from recent levels.
These moves suggest that while some analysts question how quickly Muse will become a material profit driver, a critical mass of institutions still expects Meta's AI ecosystem to expand margins and cash flows over the medium term once the heavy investment phase moderates.
Stock performance and dividend signal investor confidence
Meta stock's recent trading and capital return plans add another layer to the story.
Per data from MarketBeat, Meta closed at USD 648.03 on Nasdaq on September 11, 2026, up 0.57% on the day, after trading in a session range between USD 646.20 and USD 664.24 and posting volume of about 16.9 million shares.
The same snapshot from MarketBeat indicates that at this price the shares sit 24.6% above the 52-week low of USD 520.26 but 18.1% below the 52-week high of USD 790.80, illustrating that the stock has already rallied strongly over the past year yet still trades at a discount to its recent peak.
According to StockAnalysis on September 13, 2026, Meta shares carry a trailing dividend yield of about 0.32% and trade at a price-to-earnings ratio of 24.41, which many investors view as a premium multiple but potentially justified by consensus forecasts for roughly 21.6% compound annual revenue growth over the next three years.
Recent options data compiled by Yahoo Finance show that Meta declared a cash dividend of USD 0.525 per share with an ex-dividend date of September 21, 2026, underlining the company's intent to combine heavy AI investment with direct cash returns to shareholders.
Next checkpoints for Meta Platforms stock
For Meta Platforms stock, the next key checkpoints will be whether Q3 2026 revenue lands inside the USD 61 billion to USD 64 billion guidance range and how quickly usage and monetization metrics for Muse and other AI agents scale from pilot users to broader adoption.
If management can show that the step-change in research and development spending seen in Q2 2026 is starting to translate into durable revenue and profit growth, while legal and regulatory costs normalize after the settlement around services for minors, the double-digit gap between the current share price and the mid-700s average target range offers tangible upside potential but also embeds execution risk.

Meta Platforms Just Ripped 23% in a Month: Take Profits, or Buy More?
Meta Platforms surged far past its mega-cap peers in a single month while the broader tech sector sat flat, and now shareholders face a decision that hinges entirely on how you read what the July earnings report actually said about…

Meta Platforms (NASDAQ:META | META Price Prediction) stock is up 23% over the past month and trades at $670.52, even after slipping 2% in Friday afternoon trading. The one-month move stands out because it comes without a sector lift and without matching moves in the closest mega-cap peers.
The Invesco QQQ Trust (NASDAQ:QQQ) is essentially flat over the past month, down 0.01%. That leaves Meta Platforms as the name doing the work rather than large-cap technology in general.
Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOGL) stock is up 2% over the past month and trades at $349.99. Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) stock is up 3% over the same span and trades at $494.69. Meta Platforms outran both by a wide margin, which makes this a repricing of one name rather than a bid for the group.
Meta Platforms reported second-quarter results in late July, before this past-month window opened, and diluted earnings per share of $6.18 came in below the analyst consensus while quarterly revenue landed above it. The stock sold off on that report, so this past month reads as a recovery from that decline rather than a move to fresh ground.
The shortfall wasn’t operating. Meta Platforms carried significant charges tied to legal proceedings and substantial severance expenses from headcount reductions made earlier in the year, and Chief Financial Officer Susan Li said on the earnings call that operating income would have increased year over year (YoY) excluding those items.
On the call, the chief executive described artificial intelligence (AI) investments as accelerating every major part of Meta Platforms’ core business, pointing to large language models improving content recommendations and advertising relevance, to new image and video generation models, and to business agents and a model programming interface as future revenue lines. He also flagged a product conference later this month.
Alongside that commentary, Meta Platforms announced a quarterly cash dividend on September 10, inside the past-month window. Taken together, the repair narrative around the July miss and the forward-looking AI commentary explain why the shares repriced without a fresh operating catalyst.
Meta Platforms stock is up only 2% year to date (YTD), so a month this large mostly undid an earlier decline rather than pushing the shares to fresh ground. That’s the uncomfortable read. A recovery rally can stall at the level where the selling began, and Meta Platforms hasn’t yet proven it can carry past that mark.
Traders sitting on the run may want to check for whether the stock holds its bid on the first tests of overhead supply. Trimming into strength after a move of that size in Meta Platforms is a defensible way for holders to lock in the recovery without abandoning the position.
The other read on Meta Platforms is that the July miss described the quarter’s charges rather than the underlying business. Buying here means paying for an operating engine that never actually weakened, plus a spending program aimed at revenue lines that don’t yet exist.
Meta Platforms is directing that AI capital toward business agents, a model programming interface and new consumer products, on top of the recommendation and advertising improvements the chief executive described. All of that buildout still has to be powered and cooled by somebody, and we rounded up seven suppliers doing exactly that in a free report. A holder who believes those lines arrive is paying for growth optionality on top of the recovery.
Across the peer set, Alphabet and Microsoft both rose over the same window by far smaller margins, and the large-cap technology fund went nowhere, so the market appears to have singled out Meta Platforms rather than lifting the whole complex. What appears to have been reconsidered is whether the July shortfall described the business or only that quarter’s charges, and the answer that pushed shares of Meta Platforms higher was the latter.
Meta Platforms flagged a product conference later this month, and shareholders can watch for signs that new AI products reach paying customers on a real timeline. That event is the next dated moment where the spending story either keeps getting credit or begins getting counted as cost again.
A holder of Meta Platforms stock should size their exposure with the YTD figure in mind rather than the past-month figure. A stock that jumped this hard in a month can give some back quickly, and adding on strength deserves to be paced rather than chased. The question a Meta Platforms shareholder faces now is whether the spending behind those future revenue lines stays credited as an investment, or starts getting counted as a cost again.

Snap surged 6% on 19% Q2 revenue growth, with AI glasses and B2B advertising expanding the business beyond its core social platform.

Snap's latest results have given investors reasons to focus on improving fundamentals, including 19% revenue growth in the second quarter and stronger cash generation. At the same time, regulatory scrutiny surrounding teen safety and potential product restrictions remains an important risk for Snap's engagement, costs and longer-term growth.
Snap's second-quarter performance showed momentum across several parts of the business, with revenue increasing 19% from a year earlier. The company is also expanding beyond its traditional advertising business through artificial-intelligence glasses and a broader push into business-to-business advertising.
The focus on AI glasses gives Snap another potential growth avenue as the company looks to build products beyond its core social-media platform. Snap's B2B advertising efforts could also help diversify revenue, although the company continues to operate in a competitive digital advertising market.
Legal and regulatory pressure remains the biggest counterweight to the improving operating picture. The company faces scrutiny involving teen safety, while potential product restrictions could affect user engagement and increase compliance-related costs.

Meta Spikes 7% as Wells Fargo Lifts Price Target to $796 Ahead of Connect; Alphabet Nudges Higher, Microsoft Holds Flat
Wells Fargo just raised its Meta price target before Connect rather than after it, which means buyers are betting on Muse usage numbers the company has not yet disclosed and that this week's developer event will either validate or crush.
Published September 21, 2026, 10:24am ET · 4 min read
Market Movers desk. Editor: David Moadel.
This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them.
The Meta Platforms headquarters, represented by its iconic sign, underscores the company's massive and successful investments in AI capital expenditure, making it a clear winner among hyperscalers. © Kelly Sullivan / Stringer / Getty Images North America
Meta Platforms (NASDAQ:META | META Price Prediction) stock is leading mega-cap technology higher this morning after Wells Fargo lifted its price target on the company just ahead of the annual Connect developer conference. The move stands out against a firm but not roaring sector tape, with peer names climbing more modestly in the same direction.
Shares are at $712.56, up 7% in Monday morning trading, several times the pace of the broader technology backdrop. That relative strength locates today’s driver inside Meta Platforms rather than in a broad lift, and it leaves the stock up 7% year to date.
The Technology Select Sector SPDR ETF (NYSEARCA:XLK) is at $192.63, up 1.72%. Separately, the Invesco QQQ Trust (NASDAQ:QQQ) is at $734.21, up 1.88%, so the sector wind is helping but isn’t doing the heavy lifting for Meta Platforms today.
The catalyst is an analyst call rather than a reported result. Wells Fargo raised its price target on Meta Platforms to $796 from $640 and kept an Overweight rating, tied to the firm’s read on recent model launches and early traction for the company’s Muse assistant. That reset in Wells Fargo’s view frames how the market is treating Meta Platforms into the event later this week.
The current Meta Platforms share price is $704, while Wells Fargo’s new target sits at $796. The firm has told clients to expect investor focus at Connect to center on Muse usage metrics and on the company’s latest models, which puts the burden on Meta Platforms to deliver specifics that back the raised call.
Meta Platforms launched Muse earlier this month, describing it as a personal agent that performs tasks rather than answering questions. The tool can send emails, book travel and fill out forms, and it keeps working after a user closes the app.
Muse is rolling out in the United States across iOS, Android, the web and WhatsApp, with support on Meta Platforms’ AI glasses planned. Most functionality is meant to stay free, with subscription plans layered on for heavier usage of the assistant.
The bull case for Meta Platforms is straightforward. An assistant that books and sends and fills in forms sits closer to commerce than a feed does, which changes what Meta Platforms can sell to advertisers and to end users alike. That is a wider surface for monetization than a pure ranking algorithm.
The complication is that Wells Fargo’s raised target arrived before Connect rather than after it, so buyers of Meta Platforms are paying for usage numbers the company hasn’t disclosed yet and that the event itself will either support or undercut. Oppenheimer analyst Jason Helfstein has been skeptical that Muse will reach a scale that matters financially, citing paid-conversion challenges, competition and consumer trust concerns.
Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOGL) stock is at $354.94, up 2% in Monday morning trading, the closest peer to Meta Platforms in consumer-facing AI assistants. GOOGL shares are moving with the sector today rather than on a company-specific development, which underscores that the agentic-AI theme isn’t being repriced as a group.
Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) stock is at $493.66, essentially unchanged 0.03% in Monday morning trading. MSFT shares aren’t participating in the re-rating this morning, which reinforces the read that the tape is pricing this as a Meta Platforms story rather than a broad verdict on agent-style software.
The next data point for Meta Platforms is Connect itself, where usage disclosures around Muse and details on the latest models can either back Wells Fargo’s raised target or undercut it. Meta Platforms is also on the calendar to report Q3 2026 results on October 28, so the fundamental scoreboard isn’t far behind the event itself.
Investors can watch for whether Meta Platforms delivers concrete usage numbers at Connect, since the raised target from Wells Fargo arrived before the event rather than after it. Traders may want to check for whether Meta Platforms holds recent levels into the close, given how quickly the stock has repriced this month.
Given the risk that Connect underwhelms on Muse metrics, holders sizing new positions in Meta Platforms should keep their exposure measured and stagger entries around the event rather than committing full weight before it. That approach lets owners of Meta Platforms participate in the upside case while limiting damage if the numbers disappoint the bar Wells Fargo has now set.

Meta Platforms (META) has recently been on Zacks.com's list of the most searched stocks. Therefore, you might want to consider some of the key factors that could influence the stock's performance in the near future.

During this period, the Zacks Internet - Software industry, which Meta Platforms falls in, has gained 4.2%. The key question now is: What could be the stock's future direction?
While media releases or rumors about a substantial change in a company's business prospects usually make its stock 'trending' and lead to an immediate price change, there are always some fundamental facts that eventually dominate the buy-and-hold decision-making.
Here at Zacks, we prioritize appraising the change in the projection of a company's future earnings over anything else. That's because we believe the present value of its future stream of earnings is what determines the fair value for its stock.
We essentially look at how sell-side analysts covering the stock are revising their earnings estimates to reflect the impact of the latest business trends. And if earnings estimates go up for a company, the fair value for its stock goes up. A higher fair value than the current market price drives investors' interest in buying the stock, leading to its price moving higher. This is why empirical research shows a strong correlation between trends in earnings estimate revisions and near-term stock price movements.
For the current quarter, Meta Platforms is expected to post earnings of $6.33 per share, indicating a change of -12.7% from the year-ago quarter. The Zacks Consensus Estimate has changed -4.3% over the last 30 days.

Having a strong externally audited track record, our proprietary stock rating tool, the Zacks Rank, offers a more conclusive picture of a stock's price direction in the near term, since it effectively harnesses the power of earnings estimate revisions. The simple reason Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg is winning for investors again
For the better part of a year, Meta (META) founder Mark Zuckerberg has been in what techies call founder mode.
And for Zuck, there is much more to being in founder mode than showing up at product demos in comfy clothing as if he's pulling office all-nighters like fellow billionaire Elon Musk.
Founder mode, at its core, is being freakishly locked into executing on a long-term vision literally every second of the day. It's a true obsession with the work at hand.
Provided you're a founder with money — such as Zuck — one component of this mode is being ruthless about hiring the people you need for battle. Money is no object. Where that person currently works is irrelevant. If they fit the job description and can put wins on the board, that's all that matters.
Out comes the checkbook and powers of persuasion.
Zuck was at it again this week, snagging MongoDB (MDB) CEO CJ Desai to help bring Meta's AI tools to businesses. The fact that this happened a day before a MongoDB investor day underscores how ruthless Zuck is being back in the driver's seat. MongoDB — no small-cap company by any means — saw its stock crash.
No matter to Zuck. He got his guy.
"This is Mark. Mark has got the memo, man. He will personally go out and eat with you. He'll deliver soup to you. He'll do whatever it takes to get the right people because he knows the talent is what drives the business like his," former longtime Meta CTO Mike Schroepfer told me on Yahoo Finance's Sozzi Unleashed. Schroepfer is still an adviser to Zuckerberg while also founding tech investment firm Gigascale Capital.
Before the Desai poaching, Zuckerberg spent an eye-popping $14.3 billion to buy up all the employees of hot AI startup Scale AI in 2025. That included well-connected wunderkind Alexandr Wang, who got about $5 billion as part of the deal.
He also hired away scores of other top Silicon Valley minds with lucrative pay packages.

Meta Platforms (META +0.30%) is pushing on the gas pedal for its new artificial intelligence (AI) agent, Muse. Since launching on Sept. 8, the mobile app has accumulated more than 5 million downloads, according to Sensor Tower estimates. With Meta putting its marketing power behind the app, that number could climb even faster over the next few weeks.
Muse is designed to help users get things done. In his keynote address at Meta Connect last week, CEO Mark Zuckerberg said Muse will make people money. That could come in the form of canceling unused subscriptions, finding unclaimed property, or, more likely, being a smarter online shopper.
But not everyone is on board with agentic shopping. Amazon (AMZN +1.32%), the world's largest online retailer, blocked Muse from its platform. Meanwhile, Shopify (SHOP +1.54%), which helps brands build their own e-commerce sites, has fully embraced agentic commerce and is among the many partners Muse has attracted since its launch.
Here's why the e-commerce leaders are diverging, and what it means for investors in Meta, Amazon, and Shopify.
Image source: Getty Images.
Will Muse improve sales for its e-commerce partners?
If Muse makes shopping online faster and easier, it seems likely that customers will spend more online. On the face of it, that seems to benefit any retailer plugging into Muse and other AI agents.
Shopify stands to benefit by making integration extremely easy for small retailers, increasing the value of using its platform. But it stands to benefit even more if more of the gross merchandise value sold online goes through ShopPay, its payment platform. The checkout option is ubiquitous across Shopify-built e-commerce sites, removing the friction of typing in payment information for every small merchant an online shopper might encounter these days.
Shopify's merchant solutions are the largest and fastest-growing segment of its business, and that growth is largely fueled by its payment platform. That makes finding any way possible to get its merchants' products in front of potential customers its No. 1 objective right now. As customers shop from more merchant websites, ShopPay becomes increasingly valuable, and its penetration of gross merchandise value increases. As such, Shopify may be willing to share some revenue with Meta, producing a win-win situation for both companies.

Amazon could also benefit from increased sales on its website. However, the cost of sales through an AI agent like Muse could far outweigh the benefits. That's because Amazon has built a massive advertising business that's generated $76 billion over the last 12 months. That may only be 12% of its total retail operations revenue, but that's high-margin revenue. It's what's helped drive Amazon's overall operating margin significantly higher over the last few years.
If more people use artificial intelligence agents to crawl Amazon's platform, that's potentially fewer opportunities to influence shoppers with advertisements. That means agentic AI is a huge threat to Amazon and any other retailer that derives a significant portion of its profits from retail media advertising. That includes Walmart, which has used advertising as a key source of profit growth over the last few years.
Meta won't be the only company releasing an AI agent like Muse. As agentic AI becomes increasingly accessible, Amazon could lose market share to smaller competitors.

Can Amazon overcome Meta?
Investors trying to determine how big a threat Muse and other agentic shopping services could be to Amazon need to consider Amazon's competitive advantages. It holds several advantages that could make it more valuable to AI agents than AI agents are to Amazon.
First, it has a massive logistics network that's capable of delivering millions of different items to U.S. households within hours. Customers used to that convenience are unlikely to give it up easily, even if Muse removes the task of searching for and ordering an item.
Second, Amazon holds a tremendous amount of shopping and purchase data on its hundreds of millions of customers. Likewise, it has high-quality data on the products listed on its website, including customer reviews and exact details for each item variation. While Meta also knows a lot about its users, as do other AI developers, Amazon has far more valuable information about its shoppers' preferences. That could make using Amazon's first-party shopping agent much more appealing for most shoppers.
Finally, Amazon has tens of millions of Prime members. Prime is an extremely effective loyalty program, as it offers access to fast, free shipping and other benefits, such as streaming media. That makes Amazon the first place shoppers go, and they may check Muse or another agent that aggregates e-commerce listings as a secondary option.

There are multiple ways Amazon exercises its power. It could drive more merchants to use its logistics network, further increasing its value and pricing power, and pushing its merchant services revenue higher. It could strike deals with AI agents to allow access to its platform, but include sponsored listings in the results. Finally, Amazon may simply push more users to its own agentic platform, where it controls the user experience.
If Muse increases the total amount of online commerce, that can be good for both Shopify and other Meta partners, as well as Meta itself, but it might not pose as big a threat to Amazon, given that its biggest competitive advantage is its physical fulfillment network. That's not something easily replicated. Meanwhile, brick-and-mortar retailers could end up some of the biggest losers, so it's no wonder we're seeing some of the largest retailers partner with Meta to ensure they remain relevant.

Meta is building one of the world’s biggest undersea cable networks—it’s just one piece of a growing seafloor empire spanning 6 continents
While data centers dominate headlines amid mounting local opposition over electricity bills, water use, and zoning fights, Meta has been expanding its infrastructure somewhere far less visible: the bottom of the ocean.
On Sept. 21, the company announced Petal, a roughly 4,300-mile subsea cable connecting the U.S. and France. Meta says the cable, expected to enter service in 2029, will be the first to deliver petabit-scale capacity across an ocean. It will carry 1 petabit per second, or about 125,000 gigabytes per second, double what today's most advanced transoceanic cables can handle.
According to Meta, that's enough capacity for three-quarters of the world's population to stream music at the same time. The company says Petal achieves this with two-core fiber, which fits two light paths inside each strand. That lets Meta double capacity without a proportional increase in power or physical infrastructure.
Projects like this rarely make headlines in an industry fixated on AI models and apps, but they're what make those products run. Meta's personal AI agent, Muse, launched Sept. 8 and climbed to No. 1 on Apple's U.S. App Store within two weeks, overtaking ChatGPT. It did so even as critics questioned how much access the agent needs to users' email, calendars, and payment accounts. Muse is powered by Meta's Muse Spark models, and products like it depend on moving enormous volumes of data between Meta's data centers and its users around the world.
Subsea cables aren't new territory for the company, which is now valued at roughly $1.85 trillion. Meta has spent the past decade building its presence on the seafloor and says it has invested in more than 20 subsea cable projects. Taken together, those projects touch every continent except Antarctica.
The most ambitious is Project Waterworth, announced in February 2025. Meta says the system will stretch more than 31,000 miles, longer than the Earth's circumference. It will connect the U.S., Brazil, South Africa, India, and other regions across five continents. Some segments will be laid as deep as roughly 4.3 miles below the surface to protect them from ship anchors and other hazards.
Meta's 2Africa system, whose core was completed last year, circles the African continent and connects to Europe, the Middle East, and South Asia. Meta says it lands in 33 countries and can reach 3 billion people.
Meta hasn't built all of this alone. Petal is being developed with Japan's NEC and Sumitomo Electric Industries, and French telecom Orange is handling the landing on France's Atlantic coast. Meta has even partnered with rivals. The MAREA cable between Virginia and Spain, completed in 2017, is jointly owned with Microsoft and telecom company Telxius. Increasingly, though, Meta is taking the driver's seat. Waterworth will be wholly owned by Meta, making it only the company's third solely owned cable, according to telecom research firm TeleGeography.
These projects don't come cheap. Meta hasn't disclosed what Petal or Waterworth will cost, but TechCrunch reported before Waterworth's announcement that the project could top $10 billion. Even so, cables are a small slice of Meta's overall infrastructure bill. The company expects capital expenditures of $130 billion to $145 billion this year, nearly double the $72.2 billion it spent in 2025.
With 12-figure budgets and record-breaking construction projects, Meta is betting its infrastructure spending will pay off. Whether it does remains to be seen.
